How Self-Improvement Memory Boosts Continuous Recursive Self-Improvement in AI

The video summarizes an article by Google Cloud AI, Google DeepMind and Penn State researchers on continuous recursive self-improvement: when the model or benchmark changes, the harness optimizer loses what he has learned. The proposal is the Self-Improvement Memory (SIM), a memory of the optimizer himself that keeps the reasoning, the predicted result and the observed of each edition.

An AI that remembers its own past

The video analyzes an article by Google Cloud AI, Google DeepMind and Penn State researchers 00:00. The central question: how to give an AI system the ability to remember its own past, and how this memory helps build more robust autonomous systems 00:00?

The analogy of the video is a worker who forgets why he made every adjustment in a project 00:20. Every time the environment changes, it starts over and loses hours of thinking. 00:41. That's the obstacle the article attacks.

The problem of amnesia

The article deals with continuous recursive self-improvement (CRSI) 00:41. In this scenario, an AI optimizer needs to keep evolving the harness, the set of tools and instructions that involves the model, even after the benchmark or the model itself changes 01:02. Evolution cannot rule out lessons already learned 01:02.

The example shows the size of the problem. An evolved harness in Claude Opus starts with 68.41 points when it is taken to the Gemini 01:24. It's less than the 73.89 seed harness, no optimization 01:44. All progress achieved is lost in changing models.

Autoimprovement Memory (SIM)

The proposed solution is Self-Improvement Memory (SIM) 02:05. The memory stays in the optimiser of the harness, not in the model that solves the task. It begins to record past editions and their results, as a logbook of evolution itself. 02:05.

The differential is what memory holds. SIM not only saves lines of code: records the reasoning behind each edition, the context and the expected result 02:28. So the system understands why the previous choices themselves 02:49.

How Memory Works

Video describes a four-step cycle 02:49:

1. Grouping old editions by the recurring problem they were trying to solve 02:49. 2. Keep the justifications, the expected result against the observed and the context of the evaluation 03:10. 3. Make the two modules of the optimizer, which proposes edits and what you choose between them, read the memory 03:104. 4. Attach each new attempt, so the base grows as the optimization continues 03:10.

Results

With equalized budgets and starting points, the SIM surpasses the continuation only with the harness and the continuation only with root causes 03:30. The tests covered six scenarios between data sets and four Opus exchanges for Gemini, in four domains 03:30. One of them is the jump from Terminal-Bench 2.1 to Terminal-Bench 4 03:52.

In programming, with ten independent executions, SIM improved nine out of ten continuations 03:52. The mean gain was 2.36 points 04:13. It seems little, but the p value of 0.003 indicates that gain is not luck 04:34.

What changes for autonomous agents

The video ends with a provocation. If it is already possible to cure the amnesia of the optimizers, agents who accumulate their own lessons without interruption can evolve much faster 04:55. For the video, it is a paradigm shift that is worth following closely 05:15.

Frequently Asked Questions

Why an optimized harness for one model gets worse in another?

Because the optimizer does not keep the reason for each adjustment. In the example of the article, an evolved harness in Claude Opus starts with 68.41 points in Gemini, below 73.89 of the initial harness without optimization 01:24.

What does Self-Improvement Memory keep?

For each issue, it keeps the reasoning, the predicted and observed results and the context of the evaluation, grouping the editions by the problem they tried to solve. The module you propose and what you choose read this memory 03:10.

About the video

In this video, we explore the concept of **Continual Recursive Self-Improvement (CRSI)** and as the **Self-Improvement Memory (SIM)** solves one of the biggest challenges in the autonomous evolution of artificial intelligence systems.

Google Cloud AI researchers, Google DeepMind and Penn State investigated what happens when the *harness* optimizer needs to keep evolving after changes in the policy model or evaluation benchmarks. In practical scenarios, an evolved *harness* does not always transfer directly — as seen when a refined configuration in Claude Opus obtained a lower initial score than the seed model when applied to Gemini.

The proposed solution is the **Self-Improvement Memory (SIM)**: instead of equipping only the model that solves the task, memory is integrated into the *harness* optimization itself. SIM catalogs and groups previous attempts for recurrent failures, storing the justifications, the predicted versus observed results and the evaluation context. Thus, both the proposing module and the selector can reuse past learning and avoid repetitions of errors.

---

**References:**
* **Consistent performance:** SIM has surpassed approaches using only *harness* or root causes only in six scenarios between data sets and four between models (including migrations from Opus to Gemini and Terminal-Bench 2.1 to Terminal-Bench 4).
* ==References====External links== In paired programming tests over 10 independent executions, the SIM improved 9 out of 10 continuations, reaching an average gain of 2.36 points (*p* = 0.003).
